summary: Defines the format of the mailto URI scheme for identifying resources reached using internet mail. It improves internationalization and compatibility with IRIs over RFC 2368.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the rule for web links that start with mailto, which open a new email. This version better handles non-English text.

questions: how does a mailto link work
how do i put a subject in a mailto link
how to encode a space in a mailto link
subtitle: How a link can open a new email, with the recipient, subject and body already filled in.

tldr.problem: Links need a standard way to point at an email address, optionally with headers and a body, and the older definition handled non-ASCII text poorly.
tldr.mechanism: A mailto URI holds a comma-separated list of addresses and optional header fields written as name=value pairs, with reserved characters percent-encoded and non-ASCII text encoded as percent-encoded UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: Clients create a draft message for the user to edit or send, and they must be careful about which header fields they honor, since a link can hide what it will send.

today: RFC 6068 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 2368, so it is the definition of the mailto scheme.

sections.title: What a mailto URI Is
sections.content:
The mailto URI scheme identifies resources that are reached using Internet mail. In its simplest form it holds one Internet mail address. When an interaction needs message headers or a message body, the URI can carry those too.

This RFC extends the earlier definition so that character data can be percent-encoded based on UTF-8, which gives a better and more consistent way to handle non-ASCII characters. It does not address the Email Address Internationalization effort and so includes no syntax for fallback addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A mailto link names a mailbox, and can also fill in parts of the letter. This version is better at names and words that use letters beyond plain English ones.

sections.title: Syntax of a mailto URI
sections.content:
A URI is mailto:, then an optional list of addresses, then optional header fields introduced by ? and joined by &. Each header field is name=value. An addr-spec is a mail address from RFC 5322 minus comments, with some changes.

  • Characters that cannot appear in a URI, plus the percent sign and the gen-delims other than @ and : (slash, question mark, hash sign and square brackets), MUST be percent-encoded. Of the sub-delimiters, at least &, ; and = also have to be encoded.
  • Obsolete local-part forms, whitespace and comments MUST NOT be used.
  • Internationalized domain names and non-ASCII local parts are written by encoding the characters as UTF-8 and percent-encoding each octet.

Header field names are case-insensitive, but values generally are not. The special name body holds the message body, mainly meant for short texts for automatic processing such as mailing list subscribe messages. A to header field is allowed alongside the address list, but that form is NOT RECOMMENDED because some clients ignore it. The same header name should not be repeated, and fragment identifiers are meaningless and should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A mailto link starts with the word mailto, then who it goes to, then optional extras like the subject, each written as a name and a value. Special characters get swapped for safe codes so they cannot be confused with the link's own punctuation.

sections.title: Encoding Rules
sections.content:
Reserved characters used in a mailto URI MUST be encoded, and software that reads one MUST decode strings before building the message. A space is written %20, and a line break in the body MUST be written %0D%0A. Implementations MAY add a final line break to the body.

The RFC warns about HTML forms, which commonly encode a space as +. That cannot be told apart from a real +, which appears in addresses like bill+ietf@example.org. Producers SHOULD encode spaces as %20.

For non-ASCII header values there are two options: MIME encoded words (not allowed in a body), or UTF-8 with each octet percent-encoded. Within the URI, the characters ?, = and & are delimiters and are escaped as %3F, %3D and %26 when used otherwise. The scheme also has no variable substitution, so a URI cannot include the user's own address in the body.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters, like the space, have jobs in a link, so they are swapped for codes such as %20. That way the link says exactly what you mean, even for letters from other languages.

sections.title: Semantics and Unsafe Header Fields
sections.content:
Following a mailto link does not talk to a server. The client creates a message to the designated address with header fields set as defaults, and the user can edit it, send it unchanged or not send it. The pairs in the URI do not map directly onto final headers. Originator fields like From and Date, routing and trace fields, and MIME fields MUST be ignored, and the client creates its own as for any new message.

A user agent SHOULD NOT create a message if any header field is considered dangerous, and may keep only a subset. Fields such as Subject and Keywords, plus Body, are believed to be safe and useful in general. A URI creator can count on a client understanding only subject and body, and clients MUST be able to build correct messages from those two.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening the link only starts a draft. Anything risky in the link is ignored or refused, and the mail program should make the real From and Date itself.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC lists many examples. A subject is set with subject=current-issue, and a body with body=send%20current-issue. A copy to another person uses & between fields, as in cc=bob@example.com&body=hello. Using ? twice is wrong.

Awkward addresses are percent-encoded. The address gorby%kremvax@example.com becomes gorby%25kremvax@example.com, and "not@me"@example.org becomes %22not%40me%22@example.org. For internationalization, the subject cafe with an accented final e is subject=caf%C3%A9, and a Japanese domain label is percent-encoded UTF-8 that the client converts to punycode (xn--99zt52a) when building the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same trick again and again: write the link, and replace the tricky characters with their percent codes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A mailto URI is a template for a message, and its contents can be hidden from the user, for example behind a link on a web page that displays something else. A mail client SHOULD NOT send a message from a mailto URI without first showing the user the full decoded message, including all header fields from the URI, and asking for approval. It should also make clear that an email is about to be sent.

Examples of harm from unapproved mail include messages that break laws, identify the sender to an unwanted third party, cause a financial charge, or trigger damaging actions on the recipient machine. Programs SHOULD make sure the SMTP envelope return path is set and correct.

Addresses in mailto links on public pages can be harvested, including those in a bcc value, which may also leak to other addresses in the same value. Parsers must watch for double-escaping and sanity-check input to avoid buffer overflows and attacker-specified code execution.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can lie about what it will write. So the mail program should show you the whole letter before sending, and not mail it behind your back.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The registry entry for the mailto scheme now points to this RFC instead of RFC 2368. The status is permanent. The registration notes that interoperability for UTF-8-based percent-encoding might be somewhat lower than for US-ASCII-only URIs.

IANA also registered Body in the Message Header Fields Registry as reserved, so that the name is not used as a real header field and does not cause problems for mailto URIs.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of link types now points to this document, and the word body is set aside so nobody uses it as an ordinary letter heading.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2368
sections.content:
The main changes from RFC 2368 are:

  • The address syntax changed from the RFC 2822 mailbox to the RFC 5322 addr-spec.
  • UTF-8-based percent-encoding is allowed for domain names and in header values.
  • Percent-encoding in the local part is based on UTF-8, reserved for any future specification of internationalized email addresses.
  • The prohibition against Bcc header fields was removed, with a warning about their visibility and harvesting for spam.
  • Clarifications about escaping were added.
sections.plainLanguage: Compared with the old rules, this one welcomes more languages, allows hidden copies with a warning, and explains the escaping better.

data.title: mailto URI grammar
data.code:
mailtoURI    = "mailto:" [ to ] [ hfields ]
to           = addr-spec *("," addr-spec )
hfields      = "?" hfield *( "&" hfield )
hfield       = hfname "=" hfvalue
hfname       = *qchar
hfvalue      = *qchar
addr-spec    = local-part "@" domain
local-part   = dot-atom-text / quoted-string
domain       = dot-atom-text / "[" *dtext-no-obs "]"
qchar        = unreserved / pct-encoded / some-delims
